articles.title: Hope for millions as cheaper HIV prevention jab reaches Africa
articles.summary: Lenacapavir, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection.
body: Lenacapavir has received WHO's approval for HIV prevention

Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.
The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has said.
The drug, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection and is expected to cost just $40 (£30) per person annually.
Zimbabwe is due to receive supplies early next year, with several other countries expected to follow.
The arrival of the generic drug comes just a year after the original version, developed by US pharmaceutical giant Gilead Sciences, became available in sub-Saharan Africa.
The original version cost about about $28,000 annually in the US, putting it beyond the reach of many of those in developing countries.
Focus on Africa podcast: Lenacapavir offering new hope for HIV prevention?
Landmark deal paves way for cheaper HIV protection jab
Lenacapavir works by targeting the protective protein shell of HIV, disrupting the virus's ability to multiply and establish an infection in the body.
In a landmark clinical trial involving more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa in 2024, none of those who received the injection contracted HIV.
Health experts say the injection offers a major advantage over existing HIV prevention pills, known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which must be taken every day and can carry social stigma.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the drug for HIV prevention in July 2025.
The Global Fund described the arrival of the drug in Africa as a "major breakthrough" in the fight against HIV, saying cheaper supplies would help reach millions more people at risk of infection.

"These deliveries mark an unprecedented acceleration and expansion in access to a highly effective, quality-assured generic HIV prevention medicine in low- and middle-income settings," the group said in a statement on Wednesday.
More than 189,000 people across 10 countries have already received their first injection of lenacapavir, according to the Global Fund.
The organisation expects 24 countries to have received supplies by the end of this year and, working with the US government, plans to reach at least three million people by the end of 2028.
It is eventually expected to be available in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly two-thirds of people living with HIV globally, with adolescent girls and young women disproportionately affected.
South Africa has the world's largest HIV-positive population, with nearly eight million people living with the virus. It is among the countries expected to receive the cheaper injection.
Some 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV last year, while 570,000 died from HIV-related illnesses, according to the WHO.

The rollout comes amid concerns that sweeping cuts to US foreign aid under President Donald Trump's administration could undermine decades of progress in tackling HIV in Africa, where many countries rely heavily on international funding for prevention and treatment.
The UN aims to end Aids as a public health threat by 2030.

articles.title: Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling
articles.summary: A landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) convicted Myanmar of genocide against its Rohingya minority.
body: Myanmar's president Min Aung Hlaing has led the country since he seized power in a 2021 military coup

Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has said in his first public comments since the court decision.
The ICJ's landmark ruling last week found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee.
Myanmar denied committing genocide, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups. It is the first state to have been found in violation of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
Min Aung Hlaing said "the term 'genocide' had seriously affected the country's reputation", state media report.

"Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate," the country's coup leader-turned-president said at a meeting on Wednesday, according to state media.
The statement did not specify which parts of the ruling the country objects to.
The genocide case, brought by The Gambia in 2019, centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.

The ICJ determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were violently killed during the operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world.
The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ruling is final and cannot be appealed.
The ICJ ordered Myanmar to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure should be determined at a later date.
The court also ordered Myanmar to stop ongoing violations and immediately investigate those suspected of breaking the Convention.
But the ICJ does not have the power to enforce these demands. Instead it has to rely on the UN Security Council and political pressure to make its rulings stick.
While the ruling was largely symbolic, it was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups who have long called attention to the suffering faced by the Rohingya.
More than a dozen countries have acknowledged the ICJ ruling, and the UK has announced sanctions on several senior Myanmar military leaders.

Myanmar has been devastated by civil war since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup to oust civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021. The move turned Myanmar into an international pariah, and its military regime has faced sweeping international sanctions.
Since then, Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to reintegrate Myanmar into the international community, but it remains largely shut out of key diplomatic arenas.

articles.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
articles.summary: The musician, who co-wrote some of the band's biggest hits, had been treated for prostate cancer.
body: Watch: Andy Taylor tells the BBC about his cancer diagnosis in 2023
Andy Taylor, the guitarist for the pop group Duran Duran, has died at the age of 65.
Born in Tynemouth, he co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits, including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film; and also worked with artists like Robert Palmer, Rod Stewart and Belinda Carlisle.
In a statement, his bandmates said Taylor had fought "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer" and "passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23 November".
His wife, Tracey, said the musician "was the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day".
Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off
The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.
He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.
The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.
Andy Taylor's guitar riffs powered some of Duran Duran's best-known songs
Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.
"Andy was there at the very beginning of our story," said his bandmates Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor (his bandmates were unrelated, despite sharing the same last name).
"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.

"Our thoughts are with his wife Tracey, his children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and grandson Albie. They all loved him deeply and we ask that their privacy be respected at this very difficult time."
Sir Rod Stewart, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, paid tribute to his "dear pal".
"We made some good music together and at the same time had some outrageous fun," Sir Rod posted on Instagram.
Taylor quit Duran Duran at the height of their fame in 1985, but rejoined the band several times in the 2000s and contributed to their most recent album, Danse Macabre
Duran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs.
Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly launched MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.
They became so popular in the States that the press labeled them the leaders of a "Second British Invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.
During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station.
Duran Duran bridged the sounds of pop, funk, disco, punk and new wave with a sound that remains indelibly tied to the 1980s
The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran, after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid.
"We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy.
"We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral."
He went on to play on Robert Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.
After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.
In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion.
When the group took the stage, singer Simon Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.
Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.
Taylor (second left) married his wife Tracey at the Chateau Marmont hotel in Los Angeles in 1982
"Andy never took the easy musical route," said Le Bon in a personal statement marking his friend's death.
"His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later.
"There's a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart. It'll never close up; I won't let it. I will miss him & love him for all my days."
Taylor is survived by his wife, Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982.
"For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first," she wrote in her statement.
"Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home."
She continued: "Andy faced the last few years with so much courage and determination. He never gave up, fighting until the very end, never losing his love of life.
"The kindness and support shown to him by fans from all over the world throughout his illness brought him immense comfort and strength, and for that we will always be grateful."

articles.title: Nine injured, three critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion
articles.summary: Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as officials urged residents to leave the area.
body: Watch: Fire and smoke billows out of refinery owned by energy company Bangchak Corporation
Nine people have been injured after an explosion at an oil refinery in Bangkok, authorities have said.
Three of them are in critical condition, according to news agency AFP, which said the local hospital had revised its earlier assessment of four.
A fire broke out after the blast at the Phra Khanong facility run by energy giant Bangchak Corporation in the east of Thailand's capital at around 14:45 (07:45 GMT).
The company said the fire was brought under control and put out within 30 minutes, adding that the cause of the incident was being investigated.
Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as local officials told residents to leave the area.
An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.
Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery.

On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.
He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.
Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges.

It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.
An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

articles.title: Hamas political official and wife among eight Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza
articles.summary: The killings are the latest from a series of near daily attacks by Israel against what it says are Hamas targets.
body: Dozens of Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in near daily air strikes over the past month
A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.
Local sources told the BBC a residential apartment in Deir al-Balah was targeted at dawn, killing Khaled Abu Nada - the deputy education minister - and his wife, Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada.
A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman said that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.
In a joint statement, Israel's prime minister and defence minister said the operation was "part of a series of targeted killings" against Hamas officials.
Thursday's strikes also reportedly killed three Palestinians on al-Nafaq Street, east of Gaza City. Their identities have not yet been established, eyewitnesses said.

In a separate strike on Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, three Palestinians working for Hamas's security services were killed. They were identified as Yasser al-Lahham, Iyad Ahmed and Ibrahim al-Mashal.
Khaled Abu Nada and his wife Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada were killed in the air strike
In a post X, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the death of Khaled Abu Nada and said about 80 Hamas officials have been killed in the last month.
"No one in Hamas's leadership will succeed in evading us," he said, adding that the military would "continue to pursue our enemies and protect the security of Israeli civilians".
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had carried out a strike on a "senior" Hamas operative, and would provide further details later.

The attacks came a day after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters were killed in Israeli air strike on their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.
On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,772 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Thirteen dead as mine disaster highlights illegal hunt for gold
articles.summary: Indonesian authorities say another 13 are missing in the illegal gold mine, which flooded on Monday.
body: The flooded mine is in Bogor in West Java
It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday. Early on Tuesday, she received news that he was trapped underground.

Rais, 50, had been working as an illegal gold miner in Bogor, Indonesia's West Java province. On Monday night, he and at least 25 other miners were digging in an open-pit mine about 100m (328ft) deep, when torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow and flood the two shafts.
Authorities on Thursday confirmed that 13 people had died and their bodies were recovered from the site. At least 13 more are thought to still be missing.
Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing, with personnel using ropes to access the depths of the dark, narrow and slippery mine shafts, which are continually being flooded from below.
Above ground, ambulances and medical personnel are ready and waiting to transport victims.

"We are coordinating with all search and rescue personnel involved in the operation to monitor water conditions and assess access to the mine shaft," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement on Wednesday.
"The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely."
Rescuers have been working day and night to find survivors in the flooded mine shaft
Small-scale gold mining is banned in Indonesia, but remains widespread in rural parts of the mineral-rich archipelago.

Multiple studies show that over the past ten years the illegal industry has rapidly flourished, often in correlation with rising gold prices. In early 2026, those prices reached an all-time high – spurring a gold rush that prompted mine operators across the country to expand their operations.

This included state-owned mining company Aneka Tambang (Antam), which owns the business permit for the area in which this week's flooded mine is located. Antam have said the mine was not theirs and was operating without their authorisation.

On Wednesday, while rescue operations there were underway, West Java Regional Police separately announced that they had uncovered 24 cases of illegal mining across the province between October and November alone.

But Bisman Bakhtiar, Executive Director of the Center for Energy and Mining Law Studies, told the BBC earlier this year that the actual number of illegal mines in Indonesia is higher than the government's figures.
"[The government figures are] what's been recorded. That means there must be more than that," he said, noting that law enforcement operations have had little impact on the sector.
"It's still very massive and very big because this has been going on for a very long time."
Others allege that the illegal industry is underpinned by corruption.

Laode M Syarif, former deputy chairman of the Corruption Eradication Committee, said that unofficial mining is difficult to eradicate because every illegal mine has "backing", usually from "police and military or high-ranking officials in local and provincial governments".
"As long as these backers are not dealt with firmly, illegal mining will continue," he said.
In many cases, though, the allure of these mines is simple: they offer an economic lifeline to people with few other viable prospects.
Despite the value of gold having dipped in recent months, countless illegal miners throughout Indonesia are still eagerly digging for paydirt.

But the lack of regulation and poor construction in the pits also means accidents are relatively common – whether from landslides, floods, or exposure to hazardous gases, all of which have claimed lives in recent years.
Relatives of the missing Bogor miners have been waiting near the site for news of their loved ones
Earlier this year, in the same area as this week's flooded mine, 11 illegal gold miners reportedly died after a carbon monoxide leak inside a shaft.
Elsewhere, in West Sumatra, nine people were killed at an illegal gold mine in May after heavy rain triggered the collapse of a 30-metre cliff, burying 12 miners in total.
There are numerous reports of other such incidents across the Indonesian archipelago. But the illegal nature of the small-scale gold mining sector obfuscates the true number of casualties.

Even this week, when asked how many miners were in the pits in Bogor when they flooded, M Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency, said the total casualty figure "is still unclear".
"Some say 20 people, others say 29 people," Hamdani told Indonesian news outlet Detik. "The problem is that no one reported it and no one wants to report it."
The Indonesian Ombudsman on Thursday urged law enforcement officials to conduct a thorough investigation of the incident and to address the larger systemic issue behind it.

"This should be a momentum for all parties to resolve the [illegal gold mining] problem comprehensively, not just taking action after the incident or closing the holes discovered," said Abdul Ghoffar, a member of the Indonesian Ombudsman.

"We need to uncover the entire [illegal gold mining] chain," he continued. "We must not allow only the miners in the field to be seen and prosecuted, while those who control the activities, provide capital and facilities, store, and market the mined products remain untouched.
"Law enforcement must target the actors and networks that keep this illegal activity going."
As rescue operations continue and more bodies are recovered, the picture is becoming less murky. But even if there are survivors among those who remain missing, time may be running out.
More than three days since the shafts flooded, the relatives of the anonymous men in the mines are desperately waiting to hear whether their loved ones survived.
As she waits for news of her father, Rani says: "I hope he's found soon."

articles.title: DR Congo demands answers over Ugandan general's threats
articles.summary: Gen Kainerugaba threatened a rebel takeover of a mineral-rich area in DR Congo in controversial X posts.
body: Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba's social media posts have previously sparked diplomatic tensions
The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.

In a series of X posts, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to support a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo. He insisted that Uganda's military involvement was purely driven by security concerns.
The DR Congo's foreign ministry summoned Uganda's envoy to explain the remarks, describing them as "particularly serious" and damaging to diplomatic relations.
The Ugandan government has yet to respond.
The diplomatic row comes despite close military ties between the neighbours.
Their forces have been conducting joint operations against the Islamic State-linked Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in eastern DR Congo since 2021.
Uganda has also recently been involved in efforts to mediate between the Congolese government and an armed group led by former warlord Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province.
Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever
The Ugandan general who lobs grenades on Twitter
In his posts, Gen Kainerugaba accused the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group operating in eastern DR Congo, of targeting members of the Bahima ethnic community.
The Bahema are a traditionally cattle-herding community mainly based in DR Congo's north-eastern Ituri province.
They have historical and cultural ties to the Bahima people of neighbouring Uganda.
He also threatened a rebel takeover of Walikale, in North Kivu province, while defending Uganda's military presence in DR Congo.
Walikale is rich in mineral resources , including some of the country's largest tin deposits and several major gold mines.
Gen Kainerugaba's X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, has since become inaccessible.
It is unclear whether he deactivated it, as he has done in the past, or whether the platform had suspended it.
During the same week he declared: "My tweets in Uganda are directives that must be obeyed."
The posts followed reports that a DR Congo military aircraft had allegedly been shot down by rebels, with foreign mercenaries reportedly among those on board.
Gen Kainerugaba criticised the reported presence of foreign mercenaries in DR Congo.

"These remarks, which are particularly serious, have caused a major media incident and undermine the necessary restraint that must prevail in relations between sovereign states," the DR Congo foreign ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.
"The Congolese government expects the Republic of Uganda to clarify its official position and take the necessary measures to prevent such transgressions from recurring in the future".
The ministry added that DR Congo remained committed to regional peace and stability but would defend its dignity and institutions against "any form of provocation or interference".
It is not the first time Gen Kainerugaba's social media posts have strained relations between the two countries.
In February last year, he threatened to seize the eastern DR Congo city of Bunia, claiming that members of the Bahima ethnic community were being attacked.
In 2024, DR Congo also summoned Uganda's diplomatic representative after the general made threats against foreign mercenaries operating in eastern DR Congo.
The 52-year-old general, widely seen as a potential successor to his father Yoweri Museveni, has become known for his provocative social media posts.
In 2022, he sparked a diplomatic row with neighbouring Kenya after threatening to invade the country and capture its capital, Nairobi, prompting his father to apologise forn the remarks.

articles.title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause, BBC understands
articles.summary: Text of the treaties will be published this afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
body: The government and the EU are set to publish the texts of two treaties that were agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.
The treaties will be published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation which is designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

The BBC understands the deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.
Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.
The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the long-term UK-EU relationship.
The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
Two of the three legal texts will be released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.
New assessments of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country are also expected.
EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme
Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students
Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports.
The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.
Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."
The BBC understands that a plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.
The treaty text will also contain finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules.
Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, will also be detailed in the legislation.
Such powers could enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.
Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".
Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.
Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.
Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

articles.title: Guinea orders residents to clean up the capital months after deadly rubbish dump collapse
articles.summary: The capital's main rubbish dump has been closed since the disaster, leading to rubbish piling up in the streets.
body: Dozens of people were killed in August after a rubbish landfill collapsed in Conakry
Guinea has ordered residents to do a mass clean-up of the capital, Conakry, months after a rubbish landfill collapsed, killing dozens of people.
Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah on Wednesday announced a deadline of 31 December to clear rubbish in the city and its suburbs, which has seen an increase in illegal dumping in recent months.
In August heavy rains caused a landslide at the capital's main waste dump, with the rubbish collapsing onto homes killing 31 people and injuring others.
The site in the city's Dar es Salaam area was subsequently closed permanently, which has led to piles of rubbish accumulating outside homes and on the streets.
At a public forum on sanitation, Sanitation Minister Aboubacar Camara said Conakry was generating about 3,000 tonnes of waste every day.
He said much of the garbage was ending up in the streets because of weaknesses in the collection system.
The prime minister called on local authorities to become more involved in organising waste collection, saying this could become a way to create jobs.
"The state will do its part, but the municipalities must also organise themselves to ensure waste collection and provide jobs for young people," the prime minister said.
"Conakry must be completely clean by the end of December," he added, relaying a directive from the country's president, Mamady Doumbouya.
He cited measures the government was taking to improve waste collection and recycling, including a national sanitation fund that would guarantee financing for the sector.

Camara said talks had been finalised with a waste collection operator, with a plan for equipment to move waste from transit and sorting centres to a new disposal site in Baretodé, outside the capital.
The August tragedy at the Dar es Salaam landfill was not the first - 10 people were killed at the same site in 2017.
The government had ordered people living close to the site to move, but many residents chose to stay.
According to the prime minister, the government now plans to transform the closed waste site into an urban park.

articles.title: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
articles.summary: The Starmind constellation aims to be the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for AI computing power.
body: SpaceX is an aerospace company that builds rockets and spacecraft, as well as running satellite services
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".
Its approval comes as communities across the US have pushed back against the expansion of data centres on the ground.

Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites has to begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
Its unclear if a million satellites will be launched or if SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

The solar-powered satellite system "promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisation—one that can harness the full power of the sun", the FCC statement said, in a reference to a hypothetical society, proposed by an astronomer in the 1960s, capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its home star.

The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.
The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.

New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.
Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.
Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

articles.title: Death-sentenced Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
articles.summary: The ousted prime minister's December homecoming plan deepens Dhaka-Delhi tensions and risks fresh unrest.
body: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi with Sheikh Hasina in Delhi in 2024 - Hasina was a close ally of India during her years in power
Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh.
Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey.
The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously.

Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said.

She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising.
The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence.
Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border.
"She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC.
Sheikh Hasina fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule

India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious."
Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited.

"Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs."
India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter.
Sheikh Hasina: The pro-democracy icon who became an autocrat
Hasina's conviction for crimes against humanity is testing India-Bangladesh ties
Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming.

They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis.
The date is significant. Hasina is invoking Victory Day to reclaim her place in Bangladesh's founding narrative. Aides say she has spent months trying to keep her party alive in exile.
Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India, his neighbour, since becoming prime minister in February

Arin says Hasina has been in regular contact with party leaders and workers through interactive audio conversations on Telegram, keeping alive a network that might otherwise have been difficult to sustain from exile.

Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours".

The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain".
"We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says.

That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers.
Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months.
Awami League supporters have staged flash protests across Bangladesh in recent months
Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed.
Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control.

Awami League supporters have attacked police stations, external, torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked, external with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn, external amid fears of further attacks.

Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says.
The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence.
Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party.

Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum.

Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising".

He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter, external, proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP).
Fire engulfs a police station in Gopalganj on 17 November amid unrest following the arrest of Awami League activists

"The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising."

Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression.
The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability.
For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage.

Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained.
The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India.
NCP members stage a motorcycle rally in Dhaka on 24 November, protesting against violence allegedly carried out by the banned Awami League
A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations.
Avinash Paliwal, who teaches politics and international studies at SOAS University of London, argues that Hasina's latest announcement has "shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka rather than Delhi".

Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner, external with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade".

"The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot."
Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it.
Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics.
Bangladesh security forces patrol and conduct drills in Dhaka's Shahbagh area on the Awami League's founding anniversary

"The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation."
That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka.

"There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty, external is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam.
"For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo."
A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration".
Vehicles pass a mural of Sheikh Hasina near Dhaka University
Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina."
Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership.
"It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says.

articles.title: Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly sentenced over attack on UK couple
articles.summary: Evidence from a British police officer helped convict Ali Kololo over a 2011 attack in the Kenyan resort of Lamu.
body: Watch: Man wrongly sentenced to death says Met Police ruined his life
A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.
Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.
Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.
Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.
In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.
We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.
It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.
Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.
"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.
David and Judith Tebbutt were on a dream holiday to Kenya when they were attacked

Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood.
"My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."
Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him.
"I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."
Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts.
"I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".
The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.
Ali Kololo says he lost contact with his children while he was in prison

Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.
But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.
In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort.

The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks.

At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language.
"I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.

Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death".
"I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again."

Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings.
Neil Hibberd retired from the police in 2017

In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.
They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.
"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."

More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."
He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.
Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.
"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."

He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest.
"They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died."
For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts.
"I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives."
The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve.
"These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks.

The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband."
Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious".

"They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family."
"Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man."
