articles.title: New Zealand election: final results show ruling coalition needs minor party to govern
articles.summary: Incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon loses majority and needs support of Opportunity party to remain in power, or country faces another election
body: The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.

Preliminary results on 7 November handed the National party and its two coalition partners, the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties, a slim two-seat majority, making the election too close to call until final votes were tallied.

On Friday, the electoral commission released the results from nearly 485,000 “special votes” – those cast from overseas or outside a voter’s electorate. National dropped two seats to 40, Labour stayed on 36 seats, the Greens picked up one seat to 17, Act had 13, New Zealand First 12, Opportunity seven and Te Pati Māori five.
The National-led bloc currently has 65 seats. In the 130-seat parliament, 66 seats are needed for a majority.
The National-led coalition has the only realistic path to power – if it can negotiate a deal with Opportunity. If it cannot, New Zealand will likely need to hold another election.

Three electorate seats changed hands following the special votes. Labour won Wairarapa off National with just 81 votes, and took Hamilton East from of National with 173 votes. The Greens won Wellington Bays from Labour with 1,610 votes.

If National applies for a recount and wins back just one of those seats, it could return to power with a slim majority and without needing Opportunity. Applications for a recount must be made by 3 December, and results could take another five days.
Related: New Zealand’s Opportunity party takes aim at populist politics as it prepares to enter parliament

Special votes in previous elections have favoured the left, and typically have cost the right one or two seats. Until Friday, a question mark hung over whether National would be able to govern comfortably alongside its coalition partners, or whether it would be forced to cut a deal with the Opportunity party – a newcomer centrist party that Luxon had previously ruled out working with.
Opportunity, led by Auckland businesswoman Qiulae Wong, has long said it will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats.

Previously, Wong has said its vision for a low-emissions future, and an inclusive New Zealand, will drive its final decision. Its five bottom-line issues include action on New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly, capping political donations, a 10-year cross-party plan for health, ending bottom trawling in the fishing industry and strengthening New Zealand’s climate commitments.
After the election, Luxon softened his stance on his initial rule-out, saying he intended to find common ground with the party.

But negotiations with Opportunity could hit a snag with National’s coalition partner New Zealand First. Opportunity has said it will not strike a deal if New Zealand First’s leader, the veteran politician Winston Peters, serves as foreign affairs minister – a position he has held on three occasions.
In other points of tension, New Zealand First and Act have diametrically opposed climate policies, and Act are also unlikely to back Opportunity’s drive for political donation reforms.

New Zealand could be facing weeks of negotiations in what could become its first ever four-party coalition. In 2023, negotiations took five weeks. With Christmas just four weeks away, New Zealand may need to wait until 2027 to know the shape of its next government.

articles.title: Threat from China looms large over Taiwan’s local elections
articles.summary: Taiwanese officials raise alarm over interference by China in elections that will shape fortunes of ruling party
body: Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.

Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years, are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.

Nevertheless, China looms large over the vote, which takes place against the background of intense military pressure from Beijing. China claims Taiwan as part of its territory despite never having ruled the self-governing island. Taiwanese officials have raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference, and certain candidates have been subjected to harassment from the Chinese authorities. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.

Beijing calls the allegations of election interference “completely fabricated”. Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for China’s Taiwan affairs office, said the allegations “stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes”.

Wei-Ting Yen, a political scientist at Academia Sinica, Taiwan’s national research academy, said: “Even though local elections are not about China, the outcome of local elections will have huge implications for cross-strait relations.”

Most races are a tight competition between a candidate from the ruling DPP and the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT). The KMT promotes closer ties with Beijing, and its chair, Cheng Li-wun, travelled to China this year to meet Xi Jinping, China’s leader. Xi has vowed to unify China with Taiwan, and has not ruled out using military action to achieve that aim.
Yen said if the KMT loses some of its traditional strongholds, Beijing “may need to reconsider what is the most effective strategy for influencing Taiwanese people”.

One of the most contentious votes is the race for Taipei mayor, an office that has been held by the KMT for three decades. The DPP has selected as its challenger Puma Shen, a national legislator whom Beijing declared a “diehard separatist” in 2024. It is the first time a candidate under sanctions by Beijing has run to be mayor of Taiwan’s capital city. In the neighbouring New Tapei City race, the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui is also proving to be a ferocious challenger to the incumbent KMT.
Shen said in a recent interview that even if he didn’t win, the capital’s mayoral race was “a slap to China” because it proved that “democracy works here in Taiwan”.

Huang Bo-kai, a 23-year-old law student, said his top concern was cross-strait relations and how US-China relations were evolving. “The world’s three major powers are increasingly willing to flex their muscles: the US attacking Iran, Russia attacking Ukraine. I think Taiwan could very well be the next target [of China],” he told the Guardian.

Taiwan’s president, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing and has taken a bolshier stance on cross-strait relations than his predecessor, Tsai Ing-wen, who was admired for her ability to drum up support in Washington while walking a delicate tightrope to avoid angering China.

Lai has pushed for greater spending on weapons to deter military aggression from China. The government has proposed a record 18% increase in defence spending for next year, including for drones and missiles, taking it above 1tn Taiwan dollars (£23bn) for the first time.

But many Taiwanese voters would rather that money was spent on more immediate economic issues. Lev Nachman, a political scientist at National Taiwan University, said the national leaders of the DPP and KMT had been notably absent from the mayoral races, reflecting the extent to which campaigns were focused on local issues.

Going into the campaigns for the 2028 presidential elections, Lai would “try to take advantage of the momentum that [Shen] and Su have built for the DPP,” Nachman said, noting that support for those candidates would not necessarily translate into support for Lai.
Tony Yeh, a Taipei man in his 70s, said: “To put it simply, the authorities should do more to boost the economy and buy fewer weapons.”

Taiwan’s economy has boomed this year, largely thanks to the pivotal role that its semiconductor industry plays in the global artificial intelligence rally. The economy grew by more than 14% in the first nine months of the year, the fastest rate in 50 years. But nearly 70% of workers earned less than the average monthly wage of 49,152 Taiwan dollars (£1,137) in the same period.
Yeh said: “Most traditional industries are having a really tough time.”

William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “The issues that really are going to determine their votes are livelihood issues including the stagnant wage, the astronomically high housing price, the affordability issue, and how the government can better make sure Taiwan’s incredible economic boom fuelled by the global AI growth is going to be distributed more evenly.”
Other voters have more niche concerns. Walking her dog in a park, Kuo Wei-tong, a nail salon worker, said policies affecting pets were among her top concerns.
“People are having fewer children and getting more cats and dogs,” she said. “I think that’s something worth giving serious consideration to as well.”

articles.title: Nearly half of ethnic minority people in UK have faced racism at work in last year, survey finds
articles.summary: Figures show impact on mental health, with majority having no confidence HR will take their concerns seriously
body: Nearly half of people from minority ethnic backgrounds have experienced racism at work and the majority have no confidence that HR would take their concerns seriously, a survey has found.

It also found that 75% of people from the UK’s five largest minority ethnic communities had experienced racism or unfair treatment linked to their race, ethnicity or religion in the previous year, and three-quarters of those who had experienced racism said it had affected their mental health to some degree.

Susan Solomon, a senior research manager and lead author of the Centre for Mental Health’s report, said: “When three-quarters of people who have experienced racism report an impact on their mental health, it is clear that racism is not just an equality issue. It is a public mental health issue.”
The findings of the survey of 2,506 adults come amid reports that racial equality is worsening and discrimination is becoming more common in the UK.

Jabeer Butt, the chief executive of the Race Equality Foundation, said the research demonstrated “how widespread racism remains in everyday life and the cumulative toll it takes on the mental health of Black, Asian and minoritised ethnic people”.

In the workplace, 45% of ethnic minority workers said they had experienced racism at work in the past year, most often passed off as “banter”, while 56% had no confidence that HR would take them seriously.

The research also revealed that 42% of ethnic minority people who had faced racism linked it to anti-immigrant protests and demonstrations, 57% saw negative posts about immigrants or minorities on social media every week, and 46% heard politicians blaming immigrants for the UK’s problems just as often.

Butt said the results showed that “racism does not occur in a vacuum”. He said: “Hostile anti-immigration rhetoric, amplified in politics and across social media, can legitimise racist attitudes and behaviour, echoing our findings following the racist riots of 2024.

“The response cannot be to ask people to become more resilient or simply to report individual incidents. Political leaders, employers, public institutions and social media platforms must challenge the narratives that fuel racism and take effective action to prevent it.”

The research highlighted a gap between experiencing racism and seeking support and help. Of the respondents who had experienced racism or unfair treatment, half said they felt they had to be constantly “on guard” and ready for racist encounters, while only 5% of people who experienced racism sought professional mental health support.

Solomon said: “Our findings show that the harm does not come only from overt acts of discrimination but from the constant effort of anticipating, managing and responding to racism in everyday life. People described living in a state of vigilance, weighing decisions about where they go, how they behave and whether it is safe to speak up.”

She added: “The research also shows that the mental health impact of racism is not limited to personal experiences of discrimination. It is compounded by exposure to anti-immigration and discriminatory rhetoric in political speeches, newspaper coverage and social media. If we are serious about protecting mental health, action must be taken to prevent the harm caused by racism before it reaches crisis point.”

articles.title: Israeli strikes kill 16 schoolchildren so far this month, Gaza ministry says
articles.summary: Statement follows death of sisters, aged 15 and 13, in airstrike on residential apartment in Gaza City
body: Israeli strikes have killed at least 16 schoolchildren in Gaza since the start of November, as young people across the territory face intensifying bombardment and a struggle to find food, clean water and shelter.

On Wednesday, Gaza’s ministry of education said: “Palestinian students had been targeted for the third time in less than 24 hours, in an escalation reflecting the continued Israeli violations against children in the Gaza Strip. The number of schoolchildren killed since the beginning of November has now risen to 16.”
The statement follows the death of two sisters, Yusra, 15, and Jana Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 13, in the early hours of Wednesday in an airstrike targeting a residential apartment in western Gaza City.
Yusra was a pupil at Kafr Qasim school, while her sister Jana attended al-Manar private school.

The ministry added: “The girls’ father, Mohammed Majed Abu Al-Ouf, and their mother, Noura Ezzat Abu Al-Ouf, were also killed in the strike which injured several other Palestinians.” The father was a director of internal security services for Hamas in northern Gaza.
Earlier this year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.
On 6 November, Mohammed Nidal Barbakh, 15, was shot by Israeli forces in the Bir 19 area of al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, and later died from his injuries.
He was in the 10th grade at the Muscat school and dreamed of becoming a professional football player.

“That day, after lunch, Mohammed went to the sports academy at 1.30pm to take part in training,” his father, Dr Nidal Mohammed Barbakh, said. “An Israeli tank had advanced and positioned itself on a nearby hill before firing two rounds towards the pitch. One of them ricocheted after hitting a metal object, striking Mohammed in the back and exiting through his neck.

“He was talented and an excellent student. He was killed at the age of 15, on a sports pitch in al-Mawasi, an area where people had been told to go because it was considered safe. I do not absolve the Israeli army of responsibility for what happened. It kills every ambition within us and buries our children’s dreams before they have a chance to come true.”
On 13 November, Israeli artillery shelling killed three people in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, including a father and his 12-year-old son, Ahmed Abu Daher, as well as a woman.
Ahmed dreamed of becoming an Arabic language teacher, like his grandfather Saleh, said his mother, Walaa Abu Daher.

“That day, my husband was heading to a condolence gathering in the al-Qastal area, east of Deir al-Balah,” Daher said. “Ahmed asked his father if he could accompany him. While they were at the gathering, they were targeted by Israeli artillery fire.

“Ahmed ran to ask the people attending the gathering for help. He then rushed back towards his father when a second shell was fired. Shrapnel struck Ahmed in his legs, abdomen and head. I cannot describe how deeply their loss has affected me. I feel as though my life stopped that day.”
Thousands of school-age children and hundreds of education workers have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza, while tens of thousands of children have been unable to attend school regularly.

On Thursday, Israeli attacks killed at least nine Palestinians across Gaza, including Khaled Abu Nada, the undersecretary of Gaza’s ministry of education, and his wife, according to health officials, as attacks continued despite the ceasefire in the territory.
A few days ago, the ministry of education said Israel’s attacks against students, civilian leaders and teachers were “part of a systematic assault on the Palestinian education system”.
According to Unicef, 98% of school buildings in Gaza have sustained damage, with more than 93% requiring major rehabilitation or full reconstruction, while approximately 81% were directly hit.
Young Palestinians in Gaza face a fourth winter in overcrowded tents and makeshift shelters, with limited access to basic services as the humanitarian and public health crisis deepens.

Children and young people are among those most vulnerable to meningitis, for which Gaza’s health ministry issued an epidemic alert on Tuesday after a sharp rise in infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.

Health organisations attribute the rise in infections to the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowded shelters and the contamination of drinking water with sewage – a crisis made worse by winter flooding and restrictions on humanitarian aid.

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza over the last three years, according to the territory’s health ministry. More than 20,000 children have been reported killed by Israeli strikes.
The Israel Defense Forces said there was not enough information to comment on the incidents involving Ahmed and Mohammed.
It said that on the day Ahmed died it was carrying out operations that resulted in the killing of “10 terrorists” and “prior to the strikes, measures were taken to mitigate harm to civilians”.

articles.title: Major East Midlands road projects shelved to divert funding to defence
articles.summary: Regional mayor says cancelling works on A38 at Derby and Newark bypass on A46 ‘disappointing and short-sighted’
body: Two long-awaited major road schemes have been cancelled to divert more than £400m into defence spending, the government has confirmed.
Upgrades to roundabouts on the A38 around Derby and to the Newark bypass on the A46 will be shelved.
Environmental campaigners welcomed the decision but some in the East Midlands who had hoped local bottlenecks would be eased greeting it with dismay.
The regional mayor, Labour’s Claire Ward, said the cancellations were disappointing and short-sighted.
The projects had been approved and included in the government’s latest roads investment strategy, published in March.

The work on the A38 was described as necessary to “separate local traffic from strategic traffic, reduce congestion and improve safety”, and the A46 upgrade to “support sectors which are dominant in the local economy and reliant on roads for growth, including manufacturing and logistics”, and improve access to the Humber ports.
A Treasury review in June, however, asked for departmental funding cuts to shore up the UK’s defence budget, with the Department for Transport told to cut capital spending.
The DfT said the two schemes had been axed after input from National Highways “to prioritise crucial investment to our national defence, now and for the future”.
The decision means planned road spending will reduce by £428m over the next four years.
The two projects’ estimated budgets to completion would be more than £1bn. The DfT indicated it would still keep the plans on the table.

Ward criticised the decision as wrong on social media, and told the BBC: “We all have a part to play in keeping our country safe, but security is not strengthened by weakening, disproportionally, the infrastructure in the East Midlands that supports it.
“Losing investment into these schemes undermines this region to do what is being asked of us: grow the economy, create jobs and stand on our own two feet.”

Environmental campaigners welcomed the decision. Transport Action Network’s Rebecca Lush said it was an “opportunity for local decision makers and the mayor to work together with residents to find better and cheaper solutions … We hope the DfT will also scrap other poor value road schemes.”

Clare Wood from the Stop the A38 Expansion campaign said: “While we recognise some residents will be disappointed to see the scheme shelved, we believe that Derby can now put its energy into solutions that will actually reduce congestion.”
A DfT spokesperson said the department had “had to make difficult decisions on road spending”, but would still spend nearly £5bn a year on strategic roads.

“No 10 North will continue working with Mayor Claire Ward to support investment in infrastructure in the East Midlands, including on ways to take forward improvements to the A46 and A38 in the future,” they said.

articles.title: What would happen if Russia detonated a nuclear weapon in space?
articles.summary: ⁠Sputnik-S, a nuclear-enabled satellite, has been assembled by Russia and could be launched in 60 days, reports say
body: Russia is reportedly preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite into space later this year, in a scenario that could pose a significant threat to global communications.
German media outlets have reported, citing western intelligence agency assessments, that such a satellite could be launched within 60 days and would be operational shortly afterwards.
Here we look at the implications of a nuclear weapon being detonated in space.

A report by the German broadcasters NDR and WDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung said western intelligence services, including Germany’s Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) intelligence service and armed forces, had exchanged information showing that a nuclear-enabled satellite, named ⁠Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is stationed in ⁠the Moscow region. It could be launched this year.A German government spokesperson said it was taking the intelligence reports “very seriously”.

In space, where there is no atmosphere, there is no mushroom cloud. Instead, the energy from a nuclear explosion is released as radiation. A detonation would be particularly damaging in low Earth orbit, or up to 1,200 miles above Earth, where most satellites operate.

Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist and honorary professor at the Durham University Space Research Centre in the UK, said the main effects were twofold: everything within line of sight of the detonation could be zapped by X-rays and other forms of radiation which could knock out or damage satellites within thousands of miles; secondly, radiation particles could be emitted into the lower atmosphere and form a new “Van Allen belt”, the term for two belts of radiation that circle the Earth and shield it from the impact of solar storms.

It would be a replay of an event in 1962 when the US detonated a thermonuclear bomb 250 miles above Earth’s surface – in low Earth orbit – in an event called Starfish Prime. There were many fewer satellites then but it shortened the life of two craft: the Telstar 1 and Ariel-1 satellites.
“Starfish caused severe radiation over a period of months to at least half the satellites then working on orbit, which was not very many at that point,” said McDowell.
Keith Ryden, a professor of space engineering at the University of Surrey in the UK, said low Earth orbit satellites were vulnerable to bursts of radiation.

“Since natural levels of radiation are relatively low in this region, satellites located there are not designed for high radiation levels so they would be vulnerable to unexpected increases,” he says.

There are about 17,000 satellites in lower Earth orbit, including satellites important to weather forecasting, climate monitoring and the military as well as Elon Musk’s network of satellites that form the Starlink broadband network. The latter is crucial to assisting Ukraine’s efforts in repelling the invasion of Russia.
Related: ‘This feels fragile’: how a satellite-smashing chain reaction could spiral out of control
The International Space Station, in which Russia is a partner, is also in low Earth orbit. Musk’s proposed constellation of space datacentres would operate there as well.
Satellites handling TV broadcast, GPS and other communications are in higher orbits that are less easy for a nuclear weapon to affect.
McDowell said the artificial Van Allen belt caused by Starfish Prime was around for five years.

“There will be immediate impacts from a detonation but there are lasting environmental effects that will damage satellites in the longer run. It could take several years, up to a decade, for the trapped particles to diffuse out of the radiation belt,” he said.
Ryden added: “Just as important, the space industry would not have the capacity to rebuild and launch the required number of spacecraft in a short time.”
Hundreds of miles below the Starfish Prime explosion, streetlights in Hawaii were knocked out, burglar alarms were set off in the area, and phone calls were disrupted.
“There might be an impact on computers and electronic systems in the region of earth where the explosion is visible,” said McDowell.
Ryden added that Starfish and other nuclear tests took place over sparsely populated areas so the location of the detonation was key.
“It does depend a lot on where the detonation happens,” he said.
Starfish Prime also created stunning aurora effects as the sky was lit up in shades of green, yellow, red and, according to one report, “tremendous white rainbows”.
“There would be huge auroral effects. It would not be a subtle thing. It’s hard to be subtle with nukes,” said McDowell.

A European security official told the Guardian that they were doubtful that Russia would detonate a nuclear device in space. They said it could cause significant damage to western economies, but that it stood to significantly harm Russia as well. Such an explosion would be hard to control and would probably damage Russia’s own satellites, as well as, potentially, China’s. “It would be shooting themselves in the leg,” they said.

They pointed at Russia’s nuclear blackmail earlier in its war in Ukraine, including when Russia put its nuclear forces on high alert in 2022, followed by movements of troops and weapons. “They were bluffing then – and this looks like a bluff now,” said the official. McDowell said he was sceptical about Russia detonating a nuclear weapon in space, because it was “such a stupid idea” to commit what would be viewed as an act of war.

articles.title: EU leaders wrestle over Ukraine aid as potential Le Pen victory sparks fear
articles.summary: Slovakia, Hungary and Czechia want to opt out of €45bn Ukraine loan, as Germany tries to protect funding from possible far-right French presidency
body: EU leaders were bracing for a clash over long-term financial aid for Ukraine amid an effort to finalise high-stakes budget talks by the end of the year.

Arriving in Brussels on Thursday, the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, reiterated his view that all EU member states should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. “When the European Union provides funding, it does so as the European Union – and that union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24,” he said.

Merz has previously threatened to veto the bloc’s next seven-year budget unless all countries sign up to the Ukraine loan, which would be a painful outcome for member states that are net recipients of EU funds.
Slovakia, Hungary and Czechia, net beneficiaries, want to opt out of the loan. Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, who has maintained close ties to the Kremlin, has accused Merz of blackmail.

Separately, Germany is seeking to insulate future EU funding for Ukraine from a Marine Le Pen victory in next year’s French presidential elections. The far-right National Rally leader, who is leading in opinion polls, has vowed to stop French financial aid for Ukraine. Berlin wants to ensure future decisions on funding Kyiv via the EU budget are made by a majority of EU member states, rather than unanimously. The current system requires consensus, enabling one country to veto a decision.
In a more hopeful sign for Kyiv, Bulgaria, which had been against the loan, said on Thursday it was ready to contribute as long as its share was not linked to weapons.

“Bulgaria is going to ‌take part in the loan of 20bn [for] non-military support ​for Ukraine,” the country’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, said as he arrived at the summit. “We have a ⁠huge historic diaspora of Bulgarians living ​in Ukraine. Our wish is ​to concentrate our support ​in that ‌area. We are ​going ​to contribute, but no money from Bulgaria for weapons.”

The European Commission last week proposed a €45bn EU loan for Ukraine to fill a funding hole caused by Russia’s relentless attacks. EU officials proposed €25bn for military spending and €20bn for Ukraine’s civilian needs, such as schools and hospitals.

Arriving at the summit, Czechia’s populist prime minister, Andrej Babiš, was in no mood for compromise. “Cohesion is really the goal of the European Union and [the] Czech Republic. We will fight for this money,” he said, referring to the EU’s cohesion funds, which are intended to help poorer regions catch up with richer ones.

Babiš said his country needed a highway to Austria and more hospitals. “Financing of Ukraine should be negotiated separately. And the most important is the life of our citizens,” he said, adding that the EU should “do everything” to support peace in Ukraine.

But Merz’s stance has won widespread support, especially among western European, Nordic and Baltic states. Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said: “It’s not acceptable to simply kidnap the support for Ukraine by saying that we will accept the European Union support for Ukraine, but we will not pay for it ourselves. That is not a reasonable way of thinking.”

However, some governments that support Merz’s goal have reservations about his tactics, fearing the public threat to block cohesion funds could make it harder for recalcitrant governments to climb down.
The discussion on support for Ukraine has become entangled in negotiations over the EU’s next long-term budget, which will set the bloc’s spending priorities for 2028-2034.

EU leaders are discussing a €1.78tn proposal presented by the European Council president, António Costa, last Saturday, which represents a 10% reduction on the original €2tn plan from the European Commission.

EU officials want to finalise a budget deal by the end of the year before a sequence of big elections in 2027 complicates finding an agreement, with most concern over French presidential elections in the spring. As well as ceasing funding for Ukraine, Le Pen has vowed to slash France’s contributions to the EU budget.

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, who is battling to preserve EU farm subsidies for French farmers and a larger budget, has also indicated he could walk away from talks if there was no deal by the end of the year. “An agreement is not an end in itself, nor an objective in itself if it were based on unbalanced foundations,” an Élysée source said before the summit. If the elements are not right, “the president thinks it will not be possible for him to continue this discussion beyond December”, the source said.
The Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said it was important to get a budget agreement before the end of the year as “the prospects of doing it in the first half of 2027 are very dim”.

Others have pushed back against allowing French elections to dominate the EU budget timetable, and have said making Le Pen the focus gives her ammunition to make a case that the EU is against her political movement. “We should be aware of a self-fulfilling prophecy,” said one senior EU diplomat. “Let’s not be paralysed by elections happening in six months.”

Costa, arriving at the summit on Thursday, said all leaders needed to approach discussions with an “open mind, a constructive approach and a sense of compromise” as he called for the budget to be approved in a “timely” way, adding: “That means by the end of this year.”

The budget has to be agreed unanimously, but countries are deeply split. In one camp are the so-called frugals – net contributors to the EU budget such as Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden – which want to reduce the overall size and shift spending priorities to defence and competitiveness, rather than farm subsidies and regional funds.
In the other camp are 17 countries in southern, central and eastern Europe, which want to ensure the flow of EU funds to traditional policies and oppose cuts.

France sits in neither camp, but has vowed to protect the common agriculture policy (CAP), which benefits French farmers. Maintaining farm payments would make it harder for Le Pen to unravel the budget. On the eve of the summit, Macron said “not a single euro of the CAP must be withheld from France in the next European multi-annual budget”.

Le Pen welcomed press reports that Paris was pushing for increased agriculture spending, but said Macron’s position had “nothing to do” with defending French farmers. “The objective would be to dissuade us – if the French entrusted us with the responsibility to govern – from defending French interests in European budgetary negotiations” she wrote on X.

articles.title: Politician hosts 400,000 guests at daughter’s wedding in India’s poorest state
articles.summary: Six helipads built and feast prepared by 500 cooks for wedding hosted by Anant Singh, an MP charged with murder
body: It takes a brave soul to try to match the mythic opulence of the wedding arranged by the Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani for his son Anant in 2024. Estimates of the cost for the months-long celebration ran to at least $600m, with world leaders and celebrities among those on the guest list.

Smaller fry though he is, Anant Singh, a legislator in India’s poorest state, Bihar, gave it his best shot on Wednesday, albeit in a rustic rural setting, for the nuptials of his daughter Shivangi Singh, and Rishikesh Kumar, an MBA student from Georgia State University in Atlanta.

About 400,000 guests were hosted across 2.5 hectares at the family home in the village of Nadawa – a staggering figure even by the standards of India’s famed extravagant weddings. Guests were treated to 500,000 pieces of traditional sweets, and a feast prepared by an army of 500 chefs and cooks, Singh’s confidant Munna Singh told Agence France-Presse. One thousand kgs of mutton were reportedly used for kebabs and curries. Six makeshift helipads were erected for VIPs flying in from across India.
Kumar arrived at the venue in sunglasses and waving an orange scarf in a convoy of 151 cars (Hindus consider uneven numbers to be lucky). Among the gifts for the groom was a Land Rover Defender.

The roads leading to the venue were so choked with cars before the wedding that one guest escaped the gridlock, The Times of India reported, by jumping on a tractor and driving across the surrounding fields.
Guests were also treated to elaborate flower arrangements featuring blooms imported from China, and a fireworks display.

Instead of a DJ for entertainment, Singh planned a horse race. Gatecrashers clambered up into trees and on to electricity towers to catch a glimpse of the race, but the chaos and tumult was so great it had to be cancelled at the 11th hour. Lying around somewhere amid the wedding detritus was the SUV that would have gone to the winner.

Singh is a controversial figure. Elected five times to the state assembly, he has 28 criminal cases pending against him ranging from murder and attempted murder to extortion and kidnapping. All the cases are listed on the website of the Association for Democratic Reforms, an NGO trying to improve governance and strengthen democracy. Singh denies any wrongdoing.

In a television interview before the wedding, he pooh poohed the idea that there was anything unusual about the scale of the wedding preparations. “I laid on exactly the same thing for my elder daughter,” he said.
India’s wedding season has just kicked off. Between now and 15 December, an estimated 5.2m weddings are expected to take place across the country.

articles.title: Spanish opposition criticised for AI video of Pedro Sánchez in Morocco shirt
articles.summary: People’s party alters video of PM putting on Lamine Yamal’s Spain shirt in latest contentious use of AI in election race
body: Spanning 17 seconds, the campaign video showed the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, speaking to the camera as he put on the jersey of the national football team. “Because this is what Spain is: a pluralistic and diverse country,” he said as he turned to reveal the number 19 on his back – the shirt number of the star player Lamine Yamal.

One day later, the opposition People’s party (PP) came under fire after it used AI to manipulate the same video, making it falsely appear as if Sánchez had put on the shirt of the Moroccan national team.

The row comes as people across Spain prepare to cast their votes on Sunday after an election campaign marked by bitter polarisation. Most polls suggest Sánchez’s Socialist-led government is set to be replaced by a coalition led by the conservative PP and backed by the far-right, anti-immigrant Vox party.

As the altered video made headlines across Spain, many were swift to point out that it made no mention of being made with AI, suggesting it could fall short of EU obligations regarding AI. Others described it as the latest in a list of problematic uses of AI by the PP during the campaign, after it notably stoked outrage with a deepfake video of Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gómez.
Related: Will Spain’s snap election in November bring a far-right party into government?

One leftwing news site suggested the PP was relying on AI rather than ideas to do most of the heavy lifting in the campaign. “That’s how the PP operates: when they run out of arguments, they hit ‘generate’,” Publico said in a piece that captured some of the criticism the party had faced over the football shirt video. “They must have thought [Sánchez’s] message lacked a touch of xenophobia and wanted to remedy that.”

The incident hinted at the tug of war that has played out among political parties during the campaign as Sánchez and his allies on the left seek to keep the spotlight on issues such as housing, pensions and women’s rights, while the PP and Vox had sought to centre the conversation on issues such as immigration.

Sánchez’s video was seemingly a direct response to remarks made earlier this week by a PP candidate, Xavier García Albiol, who, in 2013, became the first mayor to face trial for racist remarks. While acquitted then he has since repeatedly been accused of employing racist rhetoric, and said he did not like Lamine Yamal, the wonderkid whose talents helped Spain win this year’s World Cup and Euro 2024, citing what he claimed was the teenager’s lack of maturity.
Albiol said he would not wear Lamine Yamal’s jersey. “I’d feel more comfortable with any other Barça player on the national team,” he told the Barcelona-based newspaper Sport.

As people across the country raced to defend Lamine Yamal, who was born in Spain to parents from Morocco and Equatorial Guinea, Sánchez joined in, touting Spain as a “plural and diverse” country and asserting that he would wear the shirt of any player on the national team.

Raúl Martínez Corcuera, a lecturer in media studies at the University of Vic who collaborates with the anti-racist group SOS Racismo, said the PP’s AI manipulation was probably an attempt to steer the campaign towards issues it saw as vote boosters, such as the mass influx of people into Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta.
“I think the goal is to portray Morocco as a threat, cast immigration as a security issue and highlight the government’s alleged weakness regarding border control,” Martínez Corcuera said.

Throughout the campaign, the PP has consistently sought to portray Sánchez as a pawn of Morocco, a view underlined by the text of the AI-generated video. The PP video also altered Sánchez’s speech to make it seem as if he was advocating for wearing the Moroccan team’s kit.

The PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, has said that should he become prime minister, his first foreign trip will be to Morocco, where he will demand that it respects Spain’s territorial integrity or face problems – hinting at a view that could clash with the complexities of Spain and the EU’s deep reliance on the kingdom to control migration into the bloc.

However, Martínez Corcuera said the result of the AI-generated video had been a form of “subtle racism” by the PP. “Morocco is being used as a symbol of ‘the other’,” he said, while at the same time “Sánchez and Lamine Yamal were being singled out as ‘players’ for Spain but not as Spaniards”.

It tapped into the vein of racism that Lamine Yamal has long faced off against, from the anti-Muslim cheers lobbed at Egypt during a friendly in Barcelona to the spike in racist and Islamophobic messages directed at the player online during the World Cup.
Related: From mocked to mainstream: how Spain’s far-right Vox transformed its fortunes

For Martínez Corcuera, the AI video also recalled the widespread scorn and accusations of racism aimed at Spain’s former prime minister Mariano Rajoy, also of the PP, after he wrote in a newspaper column during the World Cup that the French national team “does not have any French players”.

Rajoy’s words provoked a furious response in France as well as from Sánchez, who shot back that Spain belonged to “those who love it and work for it. Not to those who shame it with xenophobic statements.”

Martínez Corcuera described the former PP leader’s remarks as part of a long tradition of questioning the national identity of minority ethnic citizens, particularly when they were in the public eye. This week’s AI video had managed to tap into all of this, he noted. “As you can see, there are many intersecting issues playing out here,” he said.
In Spanish media, many were quick to highlight that the PP had done a sloppy job in putting together the video, pointing to various errors it had made in replicating the Moroccan kit.

Martínez Corcuera had one more to add to the list, one that had inadvertently highlighted the interconnectedness between Spain and Morocco. “They had the bad luck of using No 10, which in Morocco is worn by [the Málaga-born Real Madrid player] Brahim Díaz, who is Spanish.”

articles.title: ‘Trucks on fire and drones overhead’: the Russians risking the long road to Crimea
articles.summary: Kyiv’s destruction of the road section of the Crimean Bridge has left drivers facing hazardous journeys through occupied southern Ukraine
body: Russians once packed their swimming trunks and sunscreen for summer holidays in occupied Crimea, or hiking boots for trips in the colder months to the picturesque Black Sea peninsula annexed by Vladimir Putin in 2014.
Now, travellers swap advice on first-aid kits and how to avoid drones as they drive through a war zone to the peninsula.

For millions of Russians who until recently could reach Crimea with ease, the new reality comes after Ukraine destroyed the road section of the Crimean Bridge, opened by Putin in 2018 as a symbol of Moscow’s grip on the peninsula.
Russian officials have yet to provide a timetable for restoring road traffic across the bridge, which was repeatedly struck by Ukrainian drones and rockets.
Tellingly, Russia’s transport ministry has removed one of the two arches from its official image of the Crimean Bridge, leaving only the railway crossing.
This leaves Crimea-bound motorists facing the prospect of months, if not years, of hazardous journeys along a road through occupied southern Ukraine littered with burnt-out trucks.
Before the full-scale invasion, the Crimean Bridge was the sole link between Russia and illegally annexed Crimea, carrying tourists, food and fuel, as well as troops and military equipment.
But Russia’s occupation of parts of southern Ukraine in 2022 opened up a new land corridor to Crimea, along a highway that Moscow calls the Novorossiya route.

The roughly 390-mile (630km) road runs from Rostov-on-Don in southern Russia through the devastated city of Mariupol, along the Sea of Azov coast through Berdiansk and Melitopol, before entering Crimea.
The highway had already become a vital supply route for Russian forces in southern Ukraine, allowing Moscow to reduce its reliance on the Crimean Bridge for military logistics.
But that has also made the road an increasingly frequent target for Ukrainian attacks.
“What we saw was pretty apocalyptic,” said Anatoly, who had travelled to Crimea from Russia to visit his parents.

“Trucks on fire and drones overhead that our boys were trying to shoot down. It was quite an adrenaline rush, but I wouldn’t recommend making the journey,” he added, asking for his surname to be withheld.

About 5 million Russians visit Crimea each year, according to the peninsula’s tourism authorities, although they have yet to publish figures for this year. The bridge was also the main road link for Crimean residents travelling to Russia for cheaper groceries and petrol.

Passenger trains continue to cross the Crimean Bridge, though Kyiv has vowed to strike it again. A ferry service also operates across the Kerch strait, but carries passengers rather than cars and is frequently disrupted by winter storms.
With no easy alternative, drivers have begun compiling their own rules for surviving the journey.
A guide posted in one popular Telegram group, titled “How to drive the land route fast and alive”, opens with a stark warning: “Unless it’s a matter of life and death, don’t go.”
Drivers are urged to avoid travelling at night, because when “you’re alone on the road, the air defence teams can’t see you and you can’t see the drone”.
They are told to keep between 50 and 100 metres apart, stop only in designated areas and never shelter behind a lorry.
“A truck isn’t cover, it’s a target. A fuel tanker especially.”
Drivers are also advised to carry spare fuel – as much as 240 litres – along with two fire extinguishers, tourniquets and haemostatic dressings to stop severe bleeding.

They are further instructed to tune into local FM radio stations, whose broadcasts are interrupted by warnings when drones are spotted. Mobile air defence teams hang flags along the roadside, with white signalling the all-clear, red an alert and yellow a drone threat.

Even Russian state television has acknowledged the danger. On Sunday’s edition of the flagship Vesti news programme, a presenter said the road “passes through three frontline regions and comes under attack”.
Drivers were advised to stock up on food and water, and take a first-aid kit “and know how to use what’s in it”.
According to the programme, up to 20,000 vehicles a day travel along the highway.
Related: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
Beyond threatening Crimea’s summer tourist season and the businesses that depend on it, the bridge’s destruction risks deepening hardship on the peninsula.

Ukraine’s air campaign to isolate Crimea has already caused fuel shortages and disrupted water and electricity supplies, prompting local authorities to declare several states of emergency over the summer.
Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at Russian military logistics rather than civilian vehicles, and the drivers’ guides acknowledge that ordinary cars are rarely hit.

However, the highway’s heavy use by Russian forces and lorries transporting fuel and other supplies to Crimea makes it a key target for Ukrainian strikes and puts civilian motorists at risk of getting caught up in the attacks.

Ukraine carried out an average of two strikes a day along the highway corridor in the first six months of 2026, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project, an independent conflict-monitoring organisation. About 90% of the strikes involved drones.
Some truck drivers have shared accounts of narrowly avoiding drones lying on the road and say they now wear bulletproof vests.
“Guys, watch out. When it gets dark, drive straight into the bushes,” one driver warned in a message shared online on Sunday.
“Yesterday my car ran over a lurking drone on the road. It was already dark, and the thing was just waiting there on the highway.”

Dmitry, a truck driver from Rostov who often crosses to Crimea, said he had recently considered quitting his job because of the risks, but was struggling to find other work and still had a mortgage to pay.
“For my birthday last month, I was given a tactical first-aid kit last month. I toasted that I would never have to use it.”

articles.title: ‘I’m no longer a UAE official’: UN hopeful Lana Nusseibeh tries to shake off Sudan record
articles.summary: The US and Russia’s candidate for secretary general is on a charm offensive. Can she overcome London’s resistance to her bid?
body: Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war.
It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association.

Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights.

“These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. These fissures in the international system are not going to dissolve any time soon.”

Nusseibeh had a setback last Friday, when three permanent members of the UN security council, China, France and the UK, all voted to “discourage” her candidature. The UN’s electoral system requires that she secure nine positive votes from the 15-strong security council, and no discouragement from the permanent five (P5) before being recommended to the UN general assembly.

She has the backing of the US and Russia, and thinks her cause is not lost. “Sometimes, the use of the veto is tactical. Sometimes, it’s a holding position, sometimes it’s a leveraging position. There are a number of different theories”.
The centre of the resistance to Nusseibeh’s candidacy is probably London, and specifically the Foreign Office, the penholder on Sudan at the UN, and this may explain the UK political blitz.

When questioned about her role in Sudan, she asked that her candidacy be seen in the round, highlighting her role in forcing humanitarian aid into Gaza, her support for Afghan women and promoting interfaith tolerance.
Related: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
“Like every candidate, I come from somewhere, but the independence of the incoming secretary general is the key to their credibility.

“I’ve taken a leave of absence from my role in [the] UAE government in order to independently campaign for this role. But I think that if I was secretary general, Sudan would be the litmus test of success for any incoming secretary because it’s such a horrific humanitarian crisis.”

The war in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between the ​military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Multiple regional powers, including the UAE, have backed different local proxies since the beginning of the conflict in an attempt to win influence and strategic resources.
The UAE has long been accused of supporting the RSF in Sudan, a charge repeatedly denied by Nusseibeh, who has publicly disputed the findings of UN investigators.
A UN panel of experts suggested last month that the UAE had supplied crucial support to the RSF.

Asked if she regretted dissembling during her time as a diplomat, by denying the UAE had armed the RSF, or her personal role in challenging the UN reports critical of the UAE, Nusseibeh said she regretted that “the Sudanese civil war had continued for so long”.

Nusseibeh added: “But I don’t think saying that is enough for the Sudanese people and the people in the surrounding countries where they’ve also felt the impact of this war, or for the victims of sexual violence and in this conflict, the atrocities committed in El Fasher without accountability, and the use of chemical weapons against the civilian population; all of these are a litany of suffering that has been inflicted on the Sudanese people.”

Asked if the UAE had been supplying weapons to the RSF in a breach of a UN embargo, she replied: “I’m aware of the allegations. I haven’t read the last UN panel of experts report, but I’m not going to comment as I’m no longer a UAE official. In this campaign, I am a secretary general candidate.

“As secretary general, I would fully back the findings of all UN panel of experts reports and I’m aware that I think several countries have been mentioned in various reports.”She later added: “I would call out countries that are supplying arms to any of the parties, including those in the RSF … this needs a process that requires accountability for atrocities that have been committed. That it needs to be a process primarily led by the Sudanese people.”
Related: UK and France believed to have vetoed UAE choice for UN secretary general

Nusseibeh said she was willing to take risks to mediate and to put UN values, expertise and its development toolkit at the centre of disputes. Her analysis of contemporary diplomacy was that the world had descended into a default setting of non-cooperation, and the UN needed to restate the case for collaboration between nations as being in the self-interest of everyone.

The UN had been missing from too many conflicts, she argued, and she would set up a mediation board to try to use the full UN toolkit, ranging from confidence-building measures to development to secure peace. “What’s missing is this idea of a secretary general that is a strategist and a mediator-in-chief that is looking at the sort of the blips on the dashboard of conflict and saying, ‘How do we deploy to have maximum impact for most effective use of resource and cost?’ Because resources are not going up, they’re going down. I mean, we’re looking at, since 2010, 40% increase in military spending. So we’re using a lot of hard power as countries and systems to deter, but it’s not actually working.”
That would require some prioritisation at the UN – it has 4,000 different open mandates.
Her intelligence and skills as a diplomat are not in question. However, her track record over Sudan is.

One critic said: “It is a very smart strategic play by the UAE that seeks autocratic capture, and then the asset-stripping of the UN and its standards. The UAE would end the UN’s role on climate. It would be a catastrophe.”

The next security council vote is on Monday. By then some of the backmarkers may have dropped out of the race. The diplomats of the P5 may also be clearer on the flexibility of their mandates, in which case the papal conclave may finally produce white smoke.

articles.title: Israel ‘officially sanctions’ torture of Palestinian prisoners to extract confessions, report concludes
articles.summary: Public Committee Against Torture in Israel examined 42 complaints against Shin Bet interrogators over past decade
body: Israel has institutionalised the use of torture to extract confessions from Palestinian prisoners, sometimes documenting abuse in official records or granting advanced approval for “special measures” in interrogation, according to a report from the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI).
This dangerous practice risked leading to irreversible miscarriages of justice, as Israel moved to implement a racist new death penalty law that targets Palestinians, the report said.
PCATI examined 42 cases in which Palestinians filed complaints about the use of torture by Shin Bet interrogators over the last decade.
More than three-quarters said they confessed after the use of “torture or other illegal methods”, and one in 10 provided incriminating statements about other people under torture.

“When it comes to Palestinian detainees, the Israeli legal system officially sanctions torture as a tool for extracting confessions, regardless of whether the content of those confessions is true,” said Sari Bashi, the executive director of PCATI.
“Torture as a tool of interrogation is particularly egregious given initiatives to impose the death penalty in Israel for the first time since 1962.”

Over the years, in hundreds of testimonies, Palestinian detainees have consistently described interrogations employing extreme sleep deprivation, physical violence such as slapping and kicking, threats, sexual violence and being held in stress positions.

Some of this abuse is also laid out in the official records of Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security service. PCATI details the case of a Palestinian lawyer arrested in February 2019 who was subjected to extreme sleep deprivation.

During an interrogation period lasting 27.5 days, or 660 hours, he was questioned for more than 552 hours, an average of 20 hours a day, with one session lasting nearly 48 hours. Some of the remaining 108 hours were spent travelling to and attending detention hearings.

In a 1999 ruling, Israel’s supreme court explicitly prohibited sleep deprivation as a deliberate interrogation method. Despite this, the lawyer was convicted of involvement in shooting attacks based on information extracted during this period.
The state inspector for complaints about Shin Bet interrogations (Mavtan) ruled that the interrogations took place in accordance with procedures, PCATI said.
More than 1,680 torture complaints were filed between 2001 and 2024 with Mavtan. None have led to an indictment.
Other cases are indirectly documented in Israeli judicial records, although judges rarely accept testimony about torture of Palestinians, PCATI said.

In one case, a detainee’s false confession, made under torture, was used as evidence by prosecutors. The man was released after his lawyer presented proof that he was not present at the scene of the crime, PCATI said.
Sleep deprivation was the most frequently used form of torture in complaints examined by PCATI, but more than half included the use of stress positions and other forms of physical violence.

Israel is a signatory to the UN convention against torture, but its legal system has effectively codified the use of violence and abuse where it is deemed “necessary” to extract life-saving information, PCATI said.

In a “necessity interrogation” or “military interrogation”, Shin Bet officials torture detainees “after consulting with their superiors and following an internal procedure for documenting their decisions and conduct”, the report said.

“[A] supposedly narrow exception ballooned and developed into a sprawling system of legal and administrative exceptions that swallowed the so-called rule, enabling the use of violence while maintaining the appearance of prohibition,” it continued.

There is no publicly available information on the scale of “necessity interrogations” inside the Shin Bet, PCATI said. They are an urgent concern as Israel moves to end a de facto moratorium on the death penalty, which had stood since the 1962 execution of the Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann.

“The death penalty is always wrong, because it’s cruel, irreversible and negates the right to life. No one should be executed, particularly not in a system tainted by systematic violence,” Bashi said.
In March, the Knesset passed a racist law allowing the execution of Palestinians convicted of terror charges over deadly attacks, but not Jewish Israelis who commit similar crimes.
In the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians are tried in military courts, execution is now the default punishment for a defendant found guilty of deadly terror attacks.
The legislation drew fierce international criticism, including from the UN’s high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, who warned that it would constitute a war crime if enacted.
A separate law empowers a special tribunal to impose death sentences in cases arising from the 7 October 2023 attacks.
Even in rare cases where courts have excluded confessions obtained under torture, Israeli case law allows prosecutors to use information derived from them as evidence to secure convictions.

PCATI said that as detention conditions worsened after October 2023, rights groups documented a sharp rise in violence by Israeli prison guards and soldiers, including beatings, attacks with dogs, electric shocks, threats and rape.

At least 103 Palestinian detainees have died in Israeli custody since 7 October 2023. Of 10 postmortems reviewed by Physicians for Human Rights Israel, five showed signs of physical assault and six showed evidence of medical neglect.
The Israel Prison Service said “all prisoners are held in accordance with the law”. The Shin Bet and Israel’s justice ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Stop using teargas on battlefield, dozens of countries tell Russia
articles.summary: Call comes after chemical weapons watchdog confirms traces of riot-control agent found in trench hit with Russian grenade. What we know on day 1,737
body: Officials from 34 countries and the EU have called on Russia to stop using riot-control gas on the ⁠battlefield, after the global chemical weapons watchdog confirmed that Ukraine had found traces of teargas in a trench Kyiv said was hit with ⁠a Russian grenade. The joint statement was issued on Wednesday in response to a Ukrainian report circulated ​to 193 countries as the Organisation ‌for the Prohibition of Chemical ‌Weapons (OPCW) gathered in The Hague this week. Ukraine said it had documented more than 14,000 ‌cases of munitions filled with riot-control agents and toxic chemicals used by Russia on the frontline since 2022. The OPCW said laboratories approved by the watchdog had “confirmed the presence of a riot-control agent (CS)” in samples ​collected at the trench.

Riot-control agents such as CS, a form of teargas, are banned in warfare. “We call for the immediate cessation of the use of any toxic chemicals and of ⁠riot control agents as a method of warfare in Ukraine,” non-proliferation directors ​from Britain, France, Germany, Japan, ​New Zealand and the EU, among others, said in a statement. News reports midyear said western intelligence had found that Russian forces were using riot-control agents to drive Ukrainian troops out of trenches and into the open so they could fire on them. Russia has denied using illegal munitions, and has accused Ukraine of doing so.

At least five people ⁠were ⁠killed ​and three injured ⁠in a ⁠drone ​attack ‌on ‌a car ‌park in Vesioloye in the Russian-occupied part of ‌Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, Russian-installed governor Yevgeny ​Balitsky said ​on Thursday. ​In Russia, debris from ⁠drones shot down over the ⁠Tuymazinsky district ⁠in ​the Bashkortostan region fell in an ⁠industrial zone and caused a fire, ⁠the head of ​the district ‌said.

Russian ⁠forces carried out a huge ⁠overnight strike on Ukraine, hitting ⁠military-industrial facilities in Kyiv, ​the ‌Interfax ‌news agency quoted the defence ministry as saying on Thursday. ​Late on Wednesday, Russian forces attacked the Ukrainian capital with ballistic ⁠missiles, striking a shopping centre and two other ⁠buildings, mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Three people were wounded, with one in a serious condition, he said, warning residents to ‌remain in shelters.

Ukrainian forces struck a major airbase in Russia, damaging ⁠five planes used to launch missiles and bombs at Ukraine, the Ukrainian general staff said. Russia ⁠did not immediately ⁠comment on ​Wednesday’s claim, which said the Savasleyka airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region had been hit in Kyiv’s latest long-range attack. Three MiG-31 jets and two Su-34 fighter-bombers were knocked out ​of operation “for some time”, the general ‌staff said.

German chancellor Friedrich Merz accused Russia of “escalating” threats to European security as he defended ⁠his government’s plans to ⁠bolster defence spending and maintain ​financial aid to Ukraine. Opposition parties, including on the far right and hard left, have called for an end to aid to Kyiv. “It ⁠cannot be said often enough, against the far right as much as the far left: Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine,” Merz told the Bundestag. “Russia is escalating in the Baltic region, in Poland, on the Black Sea; Russia is ​escalating in space, and Russia is by now also escalating ‌massively here in our own ‌country.”

US envoy Jared Kushner has warned against a downward spiral in the Ukraine conflict, which he called “a proxy war where Europe is funding and arming Ukraine against Russia”. He told a German podcast that “it won’t take a lot of miscalculation for this thing to escalate massively”. Kushner also appeared to accuse the Europeans of hypocrisy for continuing to buy Russian energy while backing Ukraine.

Poland will create a no-fly zone near the Ukrainian border, a deputy defence minister has announced, after several incursions into its airspace, which it blamed on Russia. The no-fly zone is intended to allow Polish forces to quickly identify any Russian military aircraft and shoot them down if necessary.

Preparations for Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian utility infrastructure this winter are a top priority for the government, a Russian deputy prime minister said. “This ‌is now the most important question: how we’ll get through the winter, especially given drone attacks, particularly in the border regions,” Marat Khusnullin told lawmakers on Wednesday.

Nine more Ukrainian children have been reunited with ⁠their families amid the war in Ukraine, bringing the total to 43, under an ⁠initiative led by ⁠US first ​lady Melania Trump, the White House and Russia said on Wednesday. There was no immediate comment from Ukrainian authorities.

articles.title: Thursday briefing: Why young people are having less sex than ever
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: A new study of sexual trends in Britain has found that one in three under-25s have never had sex, a flashy headline that obscures the real reasons behind a ‘sex recession’ among young people
body: Good morning. Let’s talk about sex! I know, I know; it’s not 9am yet. But trust me, you’ll enjoy it and I won’t ask you to do anything that puts your back out before your first brew.

The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles, or Natsal, is a big-deal publication: a substantial piece of research capturing trends in British intimacy every decade since 1990. This week, it made more headlines than usual with the revelation that sex among adults of all genders and sexualities has slumped – and the standout finding that one in three under-25s report they have never had sexual intercourse.

What is driving this decline, does it matter and who’s going to contribute to my pension if we all stop having babies? (Not really, I’m doing a stand-alone newsletter on the last one.) To explore this further, I spoke to Guardian writer Aneesa Ahmed and Natsal researcher Luke Muschialli, both in their 20s. But first, the headlines.
Climate | For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned.
Ukraine | Britain will add to its multimillion pound investments in rebuilding Ukraine’s energy system by funding a windfarm project capable of powering 300,000 Ukrainian households.
UK news | Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting more than 10,000 jobs at risk in “devastating news” for staff in the run-up to Christmas.

Gaza | A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.

Trump tariffs | Brazil has said it will not bend to the new US tariff “threat” and China accused Washington of “political manipulation” in the wake of Donald Trump’s latest economic salvo against 14 major trading partners.

Back in the last century, when I began my dating life, everybody had a Number. Your Number was how many folk you’d had sex with on your search for The One. I remember this dubious social construct as an impossible balancing act – between proving I was desirable, experienced and up-for-it on the one hand, while also not sounding like a slag on the other. It was the 90s …
Fast-forward three decades, and I’m sitting in an office booth with my brilliant colleague Aneesa Ahmed who, at 26, tells me gently: “That’s not really a thing any more.”

“My generation was born into this sex positive, ‘woke’ era, where it’s bad to slut-shame women, though sadly it still happens. As for The One, decentering romantic partnership and monogamy is big among people my age”.

Attitudes to sex and identity have transformed between our generations. Largely for the better, in terms of more nuance around gender and consent, and sometimes for the worse, most obviously with the rise of the manosphere. But the Natsal study wasn’t the first to pinpoint a decline in physical intimacy among Aneesa’s peers, and I’m interested in the factors driving what is described as a “sex recession” among younger people.
Why are younger people having less sex?

There are multiple avenues worth exploring, says Aneesa, who reports regularly on gen Z attitudes to sex and relationships. “In the heterosexual context, women are much more independent, not looking for a husband to provide for them, and not willing to put up with some men who have horrible, misogynist opinions.” (I’ve written before about this ideological gender gap, with younger British men almost twice as likely to vote for Reform UK as their female peers.)

Meanwhile, young men find our templates of masculinity overwhelming or unappealing. Some believe the only way to approach women is to be an aggressive alpha, while others are anxious about making any move for fear of coming across as creepy. Either way, connection is lost.

There are also changes in the social dynamic that aren’t captured by raw data. Her peers are much more interested in “situationships”: many have never had a committed partner. They’re much less bound to a traditional linear progression towards a nuclear family – not that they can afford to start one. Nurturing friendships and platonic love has become more important than the idea of a fix-all romance.

The average age at which young people first have sex rose to 18 in the latest survey, up from 16 in 2010. For young people who grew up with much greater education about consent and boundaries, says Aneesa, “people don’t put up with disrespect.” And with growing numbers identifying as LGBTQ+ there’s less urge to rush into intimacy “with people that might not care or understand”.
What the survey doesn’t tell us

Back to Natsal. Luke Muschialli, a research assistant in epidemiology at University College London, worked on the survey. He’s 24, and wary of picking an instant culprit for the decline in sexual activity (eg, “They’re all on their phones!”).

I catch him after the initial tranche of “no sex please, we’re British/snowflakes/pick your own” headlines have been published. There’s a separate conversation to be had about why some older adults lose their minds at research like this: is it just prurience, angst about younger people’s capacity for intimacy in a digital-first world, confronting memories of how we behaved when we were that age?

Natsal cautions me that a lot of media reaction has drawn a causal link between the findings that online sexual behaviours such as sexting and porn use are high among young people, and that they are having less sex. “But our study is not able to show whether there’s a direct substitution for partnered sexual activity with online sexual behaviour, which should be the focus of future research.”

He’s also concerned that much of the reporting has glossed over the finding that low sexual wellbeing is very common among younger people. “My biggest worry is that people will look at the findings and think it’s a reason to disinvest in sexual and relationship health services. Young people are still really in need of STI and HIV support that can adapt to their changing behaviour.”
Is the poly-crisis stopping young people having sex?

Luke is foremost a researcher, rather than a representative of his entire generation. He’s keen to emphasise that Natsal can identify the trends but can’t explain why they are happening. Still, one obvious interpretation is positive: the data reflects young people who feel able to negotiate safe, wanted sexual encounters much more effectively.
But Luke’s hunch is that young people are also experiencing “a constrained opportunity for sex”.

“I wonder how my friends can face meeting new partners through the age-old tradition of a night out on the town, when their entry-level salaries can’t swing for an £8 pint or a staggeringly high nightclub entry fee,” Luke says. Apps can make introductions, but they don’t bring down the cost of your date. “Do our opportunities for sex decrease now that young people are living with their parents well into their 20s? I also wonder how a generation increasingly grappling with their own mental health have space for the human connection and necessary vulnerability that comes with sex and romance,” he says.

Back with Aneesa, I’m also curious about the substantial drop in the proportion of women wanting children, more than doubling from 8% to 17% over the past decade – an increase driven primarily by women under 35.

I’m well aware of the shift away from biological clock panic that dominated the media when I was in my 20s: is it about younger women giving up on that heteronormative progression, or recognising that child-rearing is expensive and exhausting, or having more role models of single childless women than Bridget Jones?

“This is very much a product of the society that we live in,” says Aneesa, citing the lack of support with childcare, for single mothers in particular. Also, she says, and this one hits home: “Seeing the women who came before us having to work full-time, and still taking on all the domestic labour … it’s off-putting.”

Longer-term consequences aside, Aneesa draws my focus back to the two in three under-25s who are sexually active. Gen Z are not prudes, as they’re typically branded when another survey like this pops up. But their pleasure-seeking happens in an evolving context.

“The idea that we’re an uptight generation is totally untrue,” she says. “Yes, we want these experiences, but in a safe, consensual way, with partners we can trust. And for us, that’s what is important now.”

Raheem Sterling’s rise and fall: a sign football is broken?

Sterling started playing professional football at 16, and his sentencing has raised questions about whether there are sufficient protections for younger players. What if your relationship advice came from two women in their 80s, with decades of clinical experience and absolutely no time for bad behaviour? Psychologists Susan Thau and Sondra Goldstein tackle everything from intrusive family questions to catastrophising, empathy and asking for help. Created with Thau’s grandson, the series has found a huge online audience hungry for a little more kindness, and better ways to get along with each other.
